title: Ketamine in WWOX-related epilepsy
summary: Ketamine remains a research hypothesis for WWOX-related epilepsy. The reviewed sources do not establish benefit in WWOX-DEE, either for an acute episode or for ongoing seizure control.
evidence: Breton et al. reported that the competitive NMDA receptor antagonist d-APV stopped spontaneous bursts in cortical slices from mice with neuron-specific Wwox loss. Ketamine was not tested in those slices.
Paediatric studies of ketamine in status epilepticus cover other or mixed causes.
limits: No controlled ketamine result was found in a WWOX-deficient system. A slice result would leave developmental benefit, ongoing seizure control and safety in infants unresolved.

sources.label: Breton et al. Wwox-deficient cortical physiology. PMID 34634460.
LEGEND ketamine review and evidence limits (November 2026).

graph.evidence: d-APV stopped bursts in slices after neuronal Wwox loss.
graph.inference: NMDA receptors contribute to bursts in this preparation.
graph.hypothesis: Pore blockade may reproduce the effect.
graph.experiment: Compare pore blockade with d-APV in the same model.

inference: The slice result supports a contribution of NMDA receptor signalling to bursts in that preparation. Ketamine blocks the channel pore and its effect can depend on the state of the circuit.
hypothesis: A pore blocker may suppress Wwox-related bursts when its effect on NMDA receptor activity is comparable to that of d-APV.
experiment: Compare ketamine and d-APV in the same model with a time-matched control. Measure receptor inhibition, burst frequency and activity after washout.
